title: Embryonic Development — Fertilisation, Germ Layers & Differentiation
moduleName: Medical Physiology, Research Methods and Skills

cards.explanation: The lecture groups the first eight weeks broadly as embryonic development. Its statement that the entire first trimester equals the embryonic period is an oversimplification.
cards.text: The major embryonic period of organogenesis is approximately weeks {{c1::3–8 after fertilisation}}.
cards.question: The major embryonic period of organogenesis is approximately weeks {{c1::3–8 after fertilisation}}.

cards.explanation: It therefore begins before the second trimester. Clinical gestational age is usually about two weeks ahead of post-fertilisation age.
cards.text: The fetal period begins at approximately week {{c1::9 after fertilisation}}.
cards.question: The fetal period begins at approximately week {{c1::9 after fertilisation}}.

cards.explanation: Organ formation and maturation overlap; this does not mean that no development occurs after the embryonic stage.
cards.text: Growth and further maturation dominate the {{c1::fetal period}}.
cards.question: Growth and further maturation dominate the {{c1::fetal period}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture gives spina bifida and thalidomide-associated abnormalities as examples; it does not supply a complete causal or screening algorithm.
cards.text: Studying embryogenesis helps explain {{c1::congenital developmental abnormalities}}.
cards.question: Studying embryogenesis helps explain {{c1::congenital developmental abnormalities}}.

cards.explanation: This precedes transport towards and implantation within the uterus.
cards.text: Normal fertilisation usually occurs in the {{c1::uterine (Fallopian) tube}}.
cards.question: Normal fertilisation usually occurs in the {{c1::uterine (Fallopian) tube}}.

cards.explanation: This approximate oocyte lifespan is not the same as the full fertile window, because sperm survival also matters.
cards.text: The oocyte is normally fertilisable for about {{c1::12–24 hours after ovulation}}.
cards.question: The oocyte is normally fertilisable for about {{c1::12–24 hours after ovulation}}.

cards.explanation: Acrosomal changes help sperm pass the oocyte coverings. The source’s compressed order of binding events should not imply direct oocyte-membrane binding before traversing the zona.
cards.text: The sperm-head structure releasing enzymes during the acrosome reaction is the {{c1::acrosome}}.
cards.question: The sperm-head structure releasing enzymes during the acrosome reaction is the {{c1::acrosome}}.

cards.explanation: It is distinct from the oocyte plasma membrane and surrounding follicular cells.
cards.text: The glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte is the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.
cards.question: The glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte is the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.

cards.explanation: The acrosomal reaction is not itself fusion of the two gamete membranes. The first sperm reaching the area is not necessarily the one that fertilises.
cards.text: Fusion of sperm and oocyte membranes is distinct from penetration of the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.
cards.question: Fusion of sperm and oocyte membranes is distinct from penetration of the {{c1::zona pellucida}}.

cards.explanation: They increase cell number while the early embryo is still constrained by its surrounding coat.
cards.text: Early successive mitotic divisions of the fertilised egg are called {{c1::cleavage}}.
cards.question: Early successive mitotic divisions of the fertilised egg are called {{c1::cleavage}}.

cards.explanation: The source gives an approximate cell count; stage identification should not depend on an invariant 12–15-cell threshold.
cards.text: The solid early ball of blastomeres is the {{c1::morula}}.
cards.question: The solid early ball of blastomeres is the {{c1::morula}}.

cards.explanation: This is a structural stage transition rather than merely a larger number of identical cells.
cards.text: Formation of a fluid-filled cavity distinguishes the {{c1::blastocyst}} from the solid morula.
cards.question: Formation of a fluid-filled cavity distinguishes the {{c1::blastocyst}} from the solid morula.

cards.explanation: The cavity is distinct from the inner cell mass and outer cellular layer.
cards.text: The blastocyst’s fluid-filled cavity is the {{c1::blastocoel}}.
cards.question: The blastocyst’s fluid-filled cavity is the {{c1::blastocoel}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also uses trophoblast in this developmental context.
cards.text: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst is the {{c1::trophectoderm}}.
cards.question: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst is the {{c1::trophectoderm}}.

cards.explanation: It is distinct from the outer trophectoderm and the fluid-filled blastocoel.
cards.text: The blastocyst cell group giving rise to the embryo proper is the {{c1::inner cell mass (embryoblast)}}.
cards.question: The blastocyst cell group giving rise to the embryo proper is the {{c1::inner cell mass (embryoblast)}}.

cards.explanation: This should not be equated with totipotency, which includes the capacity to support all embryonic and extraembryonic lineages in the early developmental sense.
cards.text: Embryonic stem-cell potential for the embryo’s cell types is described as {{c1::pluripotency}}.
cards.question: Embryonic stem-cell potential for the embryo’s cell types is described as {{c1::pluripotency}}.

cards.explanation: The placenta also contains maternal components; saying trophoblast makes the whole placenta would be incomplete.
cards.text: Trophectoderm-derived trophoblast contributes key fetal cells of the {{c1::placenta}}.
cards.question: Trophectoderm-derived trophoblast contributes key fetal cells of the {{c1::placenta}}.

cards.explanation: The source places this under week 2; attachment normally begins near the end of week 1 and continues into week 2.
cards.text: Implantation involves the blastocyst attaching to and invading the uterine {{c1::endometrium}}.
cards.question: Implantation involves the blastocyst attaching to and invading the uterine {{c1::endometrium}}.

cards.explanation: Fertilisation and implantation normally occur at different sites.
cards.text: The usual destination for implantation is the uterus rather than the {{c1::uterine tube}}.
cards.question: The usual destination for implantation is the uterus rather than the {{c1::uterine tube}}.

cards.explanation: It reorganises the initially bilaminar embryonic disc; the processes listed around week 3 overlap in time.
cards.text: Formation of the three germ layers is {{c1::gastrulation}}.
cards.question: Formation of the three germ layers is {{c1::gastrulation}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the slide’s “totipotential” wording: epiblast cells are described as pluripotent, not universally capable of every extraembryonic lineage.
cards.text: All three definitive germ layers arise from the {{c1::epiblast}}.
cards.question: All three definitive germ layers arise from the {{c1::epiblast}}.

cards.explanation: Migrating epiblast cells contribute to formation of the deeper layers.
cards.text: The site through which cells migrate during gastrulation is the {{c1::primitive streak}}.
cards.question: The site through which cells migrate during gastrulation is the {{c1::primitive streak}}.

cards.explanation: They are tissue lineages, not three separate embryos.
cards.text: The three germ layers are ectoderm, mesoderm and {{c1::endoderm}}.
cards.question: The three germ layers are ectoderm, mesoderm and {{c1::endoderm}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts it with middle mesoderm and inner endoderm.
cards.text: The external germ layer is the {{c1::ectoderm}}.
cards.question: The external germ layer is the {{c1::ectoderm}}.

cards.explanation: Its source examples include muscle, blood and kidney tubule cells.
cards.text: The middle germ layer is the {{c1::mesoderm}}.
cards.question: The middle germ layer is the {{c1::mesoderm}}.

cards.explanation: Its source examples include respiratory and digestive epithelial derivatives.
cards.text: The internal germ layer is the {{c1::endoderm}}.
cards.question: The internal germ layer is the {{c1::endoderm}}.

cards.explanation: This does not mean every component of the skin, such as the dermis, has the same origin.
cards.text: The epidermis is derived primarily from {{c1::ectoderm}}.
cards.question: The epidermis is derived primarily from {{c1::ectoderm}}.

cards.explanation: The neural tube is the key later structure in the neurulation diagram.
cards.text: The brain’s neural tissue arises from {{c1::ectoderm}}.
cards.question: The brain’s neural tissue arises from {{c1::ectoderm}}.

cards.explanation: These are the muscle examples directly shown in the fate diagram.
cards.text: Cardiac and skeletal muscle are {{c1::mesodermal}} derivatives.
cards.question: Cardiac and skeletal muscle are {{c1::mesodermal}} derivatives.

cards.explanation: The diagram should not be simplified into “all epithelium comes from endoderm”.
cards.text: The kidney tubule cells shown in the fate diagram derive from {{c1::mesoderm}}.
cards.question: The kidney tubule cells shown in the fate diagram derive from {{c1::mesoderm}}.

cards.explanation: The source illustrates this with red blood cells.
cards.text: Blood cells are derived from {{c1::mesoderm}}.
cards.question: Blood cells are derived from {{c1::mesoderm}}.

cards.explanation: This concerns the epithelial lineage, not every connective-tissue or vascular component of the lung.
cards.text: The lung alveolar epithelial cells illustrated are {{c1::endodermal}} derivatives.
cards.question: The lung alveolar epithelial cells illustrated are {{c1::endodermal}} derivatives.

cards.explanation: The diagram labels digestive/pancreatic cells among inner-layer derivatives.
cards.text: Pancreatic epithelial cells in the source diagram derive from {{c1::endoderm}}.
cards.question: Pancreatic epithelial cells in the source diagram derive from {{c1::endoderm}}.

cards.explanation: The source describes separation of neural ectoderm from other ectodermal tissue.
cards.text: Formation of the neural plate and neural tube is {{c1::neurulation}}.
cards.question: Formation of the neural plate and neural tube is {{c1::neurulation}}.

cards.explanation: It is not simply the future vertebral column, which has a different major tissue origin.
cards.text: The neural tube forms the {{c1::brain and spinal cord}}.
cards.question: The neural tube forms the {{c1::brain and spinal cord}}.

cards.explanation: The source cross-sections show the progression from plate/groove to a closed tube.
cards.text: During neural-tube formation, the neural folds {{c1::fuse}}.
cards.question: During neural-tube formation, the neural folds {{c1::fuse}}.

cards.explanation: The blocks are called somites and help establish the segmented axial body plan.
cards.text: Segmentation of mesoderm into paired blocks is {{c1::somitogenesis}}.
cards.question: Segmentation of mesoderm into paired blocks is {{c1::somitogenesis}}.

cards.explanation: They contribute to axial skeletal and associated muscle/connective-tissue organisation.
cards.text: Somites form along the embryo’s {{c1::anterior–posterior axis}}.
cards.question: Somites form along the embryo’s {{c1::anterior–posterior axis}}.

cards.explanation: The slide lists cartilage, bone, muscle and tendon. This is not a claim that somites generate every skeletal structure in the body.
cards.text: Somite derivatives include axial skeletal tissues and {{c1::skeletal muscle}}.
cards.question: Somite derivatives include axial skeletal tissues and {{c1::skeletal muscle}}.

cards.explanation: The slide groups folding with the week-3 processes, but much of the major body folding occurs during week 4.
cards.text: Embryonic folding changes the flatter disc into a curved {{c1::C-shaped body}}.
cards.question: Embryonic folding changes the flatter disc into a curved {{c1::C-shaped body}}.

cards.explanation: This is a change in three-dimensional arrangement rather than a new germ layer.
cards.text: Folding helps turn part of the embryonic endoderm into the primitive {{c1::gut tube}}.
cards.question: Folding helps turn part of the embryonic endoderm into the primitive {{c1::gut tube}}.

cards.explanation: The source includes human imaging links and a chick-heart demonstration; these do not make the chick image a human embryo measurement.
cards.text: The week-4 overview highlights formation of the {{c1::heart}}.
cards.question: The week-4 overview highlights formation of the {{c1::heart}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture’s week-4 overview mentions cavities, but some extraembryonic structures begin forming earlier; they do not all first appear in week 4.
cards.text: Structures outside the embryo proper are described as {{c1::extraembryonic}}.
cards.question: Structures outside the embryo proper are described as {{c1::extraembryonic}}.

cards.explanation: The week-5–8 images illustrate progressively developing organs, tissues and limbs.
cards.text: Formation of organs during embryonic development is {{c1::organogenesis}}.
cards.question: Formation of organs during embryonic development is {{c1::organogenesis}}.

cards.explanation: Species-specific timing and anatomy still differ; the unkeyed mouse-versus-human comparison is not used to guess species from appearance alone.
cards.text: Similar early developmental processes across species permit use of {{c1::animal models}}.
cards.question: Similar early developmental processes across species permit use of {{c1::animal models}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the slide: these patterns are not simply maps of neural-crest migration. They can reveal clonal skin-cell distributions when genetic/epigenetic differences become visible.
cards.text: Blaschko’s lines can reflect patterns of embryonic skin-cell {{c1::mosaicism}}.
cards.question: Blaschko’s lines can reflect patterns of embryonic skin-cell {{c1::mosaicism}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture distinguishes this from later development of reproductive anatomy in response to downstream signals.
cards.text: The genetic/gonadal initiation process is termed sex {{c1::determination}}.
cards.question: The genetic/gonadal initiation process is termed sex {{c1::determination}}.

cards.explanation: Determination and differentiation are related developmental stages, not synonyms.
cards.text: Development of reproductive anatomy in response to genes and hormones is sex {{c1::differentiation}}.
cards.question: Development of reproductive anatomy in response to genes and hormones is sex {{c1::differentiation}}.

cards.explanation: They are arranged into 23 pairs; aneuploidies and mosaicism are exceptions, not excluded by the word “typical”.
cards.text: A typical human diploid somatic cell contains {{c1::46 chromosomes}}.
cards.question: A typical human diploid somatic cell contains {{c1::46 chromosomes}}.

cards.explanation: The remaining pair comprises sex chromosomes.
cards.text: The number of autosomal pairs in a typical human karyotype is {{c1::22}}.
cards.question: The number of autosomal pairs in a typical human karyotype is {{c1::22}}.

cards.explanation: Chromosomes are one component of sex development, not a complete prediction of every person’s gonadal or anatomical characteristics.
cards.text: The common karyotypes associated with typical female and male development are {{c1::46,XX and 46,XY}}, respectively.
cards.question: The common karyotypes associated with typical female and male development are {{c1::46,XX and 46,XY}}, respectively.

cards.explanation: Its importance is not limited to sex determination or gamete formation.
cards.text: The X chromosome carries genes with many {{c1::non-reproductive functions}}.
cards.question: The X chromosome carries genes with many {{c1::non-reproductive functions}}.

cards.explanation: In many XX somatic cells, one X is largely inactivated. Some genes escape inactivation, and the process is not identical in every cell type.
cards.text: A condensed inactive X chromosome is called a {{c1::Barr body}}.
cards.question: A condensed inactive X chromosome is called a {{c1::Barr body}}.

cards.explanation: Descendants tend to retain the same inactive X; skewing can occur, so random initiation does not guarantee a perfect 50:50 tissue ratio.
cards.text: Early random X inactivation can create clonal {{c1::mosaicism}} in XX tissues.
cards.question: Early random X inactivation can create clonal {{c1::mosaicism}} in XX tissues.

cards.explanation: The figure is a model of X-linked mosaic expression, not proof that every coat colour locus is X-linked.
cards.text: The tortoiseshell-cat example illustrates differential expression from {{c1::active X chromosomes}} in different cell clones.
cards.question: The tortoiseshell-cat example illustrates differential expression from {{c1::active X chromosomes}} in different cell clones.

cards.explanation: The slide’s broad “X-linked disorders” label is refined: dominant X-linked conditions and affected XX individuals also exist.
cards.text: X-linked recessive variants often manifest in XY individuals because they are {{c1::hemizygous for most X-linked genes}}.
cards.question: X-linked recessive variants often manifest in XY individuals because they are {{c1::hemizygous for most X-linked genes}}.

cards.explanation: The source also lists red–green colour-vision deficiency. Its numerical incidence estimates are not treated as universal current values.
cards.text: Haemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are examples used to illustrate {{c1::X-linked recessive inheritance}}.
cards.question: Haemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are examples used to illustrate {{c1::X-linked recessive inheritance}}.

cards.explanation: It illustrates that an additional X does not by itself replace the usual testis-determining pathway. Individual features and mosaic forms vary.
cards.text: The common Klinefelter karyotype shown is {{c1::47,XXY}}.
cards.question: The common Klinefelter karyotype shown is {{c1::47,XXY}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses X0 notation. Clinical presentation varies and not all Turner cases have the same chromosome pattern.
cards.text: The common Turner karyotype shown is {{c1::45,X}}.
cards.question: The common Turner karyotype shown is {{c1::45,X}}.

cards.explanation: Early reproductive structures share a common plan rather than being mature ovaries or testes from the outset.
cards.text: The early gonad capable of following different developmental pathways is {{c1::bipotential}}.
cards.question: The early gonad capable of following different developmental pathways is {{c1::bipotential}}.

cards.explanation: The source calls this the sex-determining region of the Y. It is a gene-level developmental trigger, not a claim that a Y chromosome always guarantees one complete phenotype.
cards.text: The Y-associated gene usually initiating testis differentiation is {{c1::SRY}}.
cards.question: The Y-associated gene usually initiating testis differentiation is {{c1::SRY}}.

cards.explanation: Many downstream genes are on other chromosomes; the pathway is not encoded solely by Y-linked genes.
cards.text: SRY acts through a gene-regulatory pathway promoting {{c1::testis development}}.
cards.question: SRY acts through a gene-regulatory pathway promoting {{c1::testis development}}.

cards.explanation: Functional determination, hormone production and tissue responsiveness all matter. The source’s headline is a useful simplified model, not an exceptionless rule.
cards.text: The presence of a Y chromosome alone is {{c1::not sufficient to predict all anatomy}}.
cards.question: The presence of a Y chromosome alone is {{c1::not sufficient to predict all anatomy}}.
cards.answer: not sufficient to predict all anatomy

cards.explanation: The early diagram shows it alongside the Müllerian duct.
cards.text: The Wolffian duct is also called the {{c1::mesonephric duct}}.
cards.question: The Wolffian duct is also called the {{c1::mesonephric duct}}.

cards.explanation: The name distinguishes it from the Wolffian/mesonephric system.
cards.text: The Müllerian duct is also called the {{c1::paramesonephric duct}}.
cards.question: The Müllerian duct is also called the {{c1::paramesonephric duct}}.

cards.explanation: These form structures such as the epididymis, ductus deferens and seminal vesicles.
cards.text: Testosterone supports development of the {{c1::Wolffian ducts}}.
cards.question: Testosterone supports development of the {{c1::Wolffian ducts}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the Müllerian-derived uterine tube.
cards.text: A Wolffian-derived sperm-conducting duct is the {{c1::ductus (vas) deferens}}.
cards.question: A Wolffian-derived sperm-conducting duct is the {{c1::ductus (vas) deferens}}.

cards.explanation: The source also labels cervix and upper vaginal contributions; the exact fraction of vaginal origin is not used as an invariant rule.
cards.text: In the absence of AMH action, Müllerian ducts can form the uterus and {{c1::uterine tubes}}.
cards.question: In the absence of AMH action, Müllerian ducts can form the uterus and {{c1::uterine tubes}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the AMH-mediated regression of Müllerian ducts.
cards.text: Without adequate testosterone support, Wolffian ducts typically {{c1::regress}}.
cards.question: Without adequate testosterone support, Wolffian ducts typically {{c1::regress}}.

cards.explanation: This is not the same as testosterone’s support of the internal Wolffian ducts.
cards.text: DHT supports typical development of {{c1::male external genitalia}}.
cards.question: DHT supports typical development of {{c1::male external genitalia}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram shows homologous starting structures rather than two unrelated embryonic origins.
cards.text: The shared early structure giving rise to the clitoris or glans penis is the {{c1::genital tubercle}}.
cards.question: The shared early structure giving rise to the clitoris or glans penis is the {{c1::genital tubercle}}.

cards.explanation: The figure’s broader penile-shaft wording is simplified; the paired swellings are classically linked with labioscrotal derivatives.
cards.text: The labioscrotal swellings contribute to the labia majora or {{c1::scrotum}}.
cards.question: The labioscrotal swellings contribute to the labia majora or {{c1::scrotum}}.

cards.explanation: Their development differs from labioscrotal swellings, which contribute to the labia majora.
cards.text: The unfused urogenital folds contribute to the {{c1::labia minora}}.
cards.question: The unfused urogenital folds contribute to the {{c1::labia minora}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses a broad shaft description; the card distinguishes the fold contribution from the labioscrotal contribution.
cards.text: Fusion of the urogenital folds contributes to the penile {{c1::urethral enclosure}}.
cards.question: Fusion of the urogenital folds contributes to the penile {{c1::urethral enclosure}}.

cards.explanation: AMH is also called Müllerian-inhibiting substance in this lecture.
cards.text: The testicular cells secreting anti-Müllerian hormone are {{c1::Sertoli cells}}.
cards.question: The testicular cells secreting anti-Müllerian hormone are {{c1::Sertoli cells}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with Sertoli-cell AMH production.
cards.text: Testosterone is produced by fetal testicular {{c1::Leydig cells}}.
cards.question: Testosterone is produced by fetal testicular {{c1::Leydig cells}}.

cards.explanation: The source’s “attacks female structures” wording is replaced by the specific developmental target; AMH does not remove every structure associated with female anatomy.
cards.text: AMH causes regression of the {{c1::Müllerian ducts}}.
cards.question: AMH causes regression of the {{c1::Müllerian ducts}}.

cards.explanation: DHT means dihydrotestosterone; conversion changes local androgen signalling.
cards.text: The enzyme converting testosterone to DHT is {{c1::5α-reductase}}.
cards.question: The enzyme converting testosterone to DHT is {{c1::5α-reductase}}.

cards.explanation: It is a potent androgen formed from testosterone, with important roles in external genital differentiation.
cards.text: Dihydrotestosterone is abbreviated {{c1::DHT}}.
cards.question: Dihydrotestosterone is abbreviated {{c1::DHT}}.

cards.explanation: The final diagrams include DHT-related prostate/external genital development. This is not a claim that the prostate derives from the Wolffian duct.
cards.text: The prostate is associated with androgen-dependent {{c1::male differentiation}}.
cards.question: The prostate is associated with androgen-dependent {{c1::male differentiation}}.

cards.explanation: The source distinguishes this stage from initiation of gonadal determination. A diagnostic label still requires more than the diagram alone.
cards.text: A defect in hormone production or response after gonadal determination primarily affects sexual {{c1::differentiation}}.
cards.question: A defect in hormone production or response after gonadal determination primarily affects sexual {{c1::differentiation}}.

cards.explanation: This follows from separating determination, hormone secretion and target-tissue response; no unprovided case diagnosis is inferred.
cards.text: Normal SRY-driven testis formation does not guarantee normal downstream {{c1::androgen responsiveness}}.
cards.question: Normal SRY-driven testis formation does not guarantee normal downstream {{c1::androgen responsiveness}}.

• Second and Third Trimesters = fetal period (growth)
UNSW Embryology

slides.topic: Embryonic Development — Fertilisation, Germ Layers & Differentiation — page 7
slides.text:
Why study embryonic development?
• Understanding health of developing babies
• Genetic and birth disorders often affect embryonic 
development e.g. spina bifida, thalidomide syndrome
• Supporting fertility research and therapies
• Understanding how organs and tissues are made
• Embryonic processes often re-occur later in life e.g. 
cancer, cell regeneration

slides.topic: Embryonic Development — Fertilisation, Germ Layers & Differentiation — page 9
slides.text:
• An egg can be fertilized for only about 12–24 hours after ovulation
• Fertilization normally takes place in the Fallopian tube
• Only about 100 sperm reach this point
• The first sperm to reach the ovum finds sperm-binding receptors on the 
oocyte membrane and binds to the ovum
• Sperm release enzymes from the acrosome in the sperm head, 
acrosomal reaction > the enzymes dissolve cell junctions and the zona 
pellucida
Fertilisation

slides.text:
Week 3: Four important processes occur
Embryonic disc (2 layered)
The embryonic disc undergoes 4 important processes, that form 
the overall plan of the body:
• Gastrulation 
 
the formation of the 3-layer embryo
• Neurulation  
 
starts to form the neural tissue
• Somitogenesis  
forms the axial body plan
• Folding  
 
 
folding to form a tube and a C-shape embryo

X-linked disorders

Colour blindness (1/10 males)

slides.topic: Embryonic Development — Fertilisation, Germ Layers & Differentiation — page 34
slides.text:
The presence of a Y chromosome causes male anatomy 
to develop
• Up until about 6 weeks gestation - male and female 
embryos are identical anatomically (the ‘bipotential’ stage)
• At about 7 weeks, male foetus starts to develop testes
• Triggered by expression of the SRY gene on the Y 
chromosome (Sex Determining Region of the Y 
chromosome)
• Expression of the SRY gene leads to production of 
transcription factors → expression of other genes on the 
other chromosomes → causes development of the testes
